pillar_reactions.evidence: The most engaged pillar reaction in the batch. The rep opened it correctly for this prospect — mobility as the foundation that lets him add load to his existing calisthenics, 'if you are mobile, you're getting stronger, your joints are getting more adapted to the more weight that you can actually push, or even in calisthenics, get more weight on the dips' — and then made the key promise, that kettlebell and calisthenics days 'complement each other naturally. So you don't have to replace anything that you've built.' The prospect took the pillar over: he described in full detail the 30-minute EMOM he had done that same day (five snatches per arm, fifteen push-ups, five thrusters per side, five pull-ups) and what it exposed — 'push-ups and pull-ups are easy. But thrusters, I'm not actually too used to using the core as the thruster needs to be used... I was absolutely torched when I finished it, but it was good.' He also volunteered the aspiration outright: 'that body, Trevor's body, it's the way I want to be built. It's a decent amount of muscle mass, very low fat, really capable. That kind of body is my goal body.' Unambiguously enthusiastic on both tests.

Pre-conceded as usual — 'from what I understood, you basically have it almost dialed in' — but this time the pillar hit an existing conviction rather than dead air. When the rep mentioned the eating window, the prospect ran with it unprompted and at length: 'I can't stress enough fasting because I think it's something so incredible. In the day that I'm fasting, I don't have low energy. I work more. The mind works very clearly. The mind is sharp. I can read like 10 articles and absorb all of them.' He had already volunteered that Trevor's fasting protocol, not just the kettlebells, was what drew him to the channel, and that he fasts 24 to 36 hours every one to two weeks and treats it as 'a cleansing day, a spiritual thing.' The pillar required no selling because the prospect was already practising a stricter version of it, which is worth noting for the rollup: this is alignment, not persuasion.

Well positioned against the one thing this prospect could not solve himself — 'when your second child will appear in this world, you're probably going to have less time and less sleep... there probably may be times that you could fall off. And here's where the accountability comes in.' Delivered direct phone access, over-communication, weekly check-ins and schedule rebuilding around the newborn. The response was polite and brief: 'Okay... That makes sense? Okay. Yeah. A lot.' Scored accepted rather than enthusiastic on the pillar itself, though he endorsed its value explicitly later, while declining on price: 'for Trevor's work and for the accountability, I think actually that is pretty fair.' That is the most useful sentence on the call — the accountability layer was valued at the price asked, and the transaction still failed on currency.

anchors.raw: when we have to deal in Brazilian [reais], when we make the conversion it's about probably something along the lines of 25 to 28,000... it's a lot for right now, even 4K, because that will mean something close to 20,000.
anchors.note: The decisive anchor and the third instance of this exact pattern in four sales calls in this batch, after NZ$7,500 and a Danish salary comparison. A flat USD price is being sold worldwide with no local framing, no regional pricing and no acknowledgement when the prospect does the arithmetic out loud. Here it defeated a physician — the ICP's own headline occupation — who had already agreed the price was fair. The rep did not respond to the conversion at all, on either the $6,000 or the $4,000 figure.

anchors.raw: it's something that I definitely look forward to do in some time because I don't think it's an absurd value. And I think for that, for Trevor's work and for the accountability, I think actually that is pretty fair.
anchors.note: A prospect validating the price while declining it. This removes value, positioning and trust from the list of causes and leaves only cashflow and currency, which makes this the cleanest affordability loss in the batch. It also means the relationship is genuinely re-openable, unlike a loss where the prospect concluded the offer was overpriced.

anchors.raw: we already committed to a lot of expenses right now due to we moving to a different apartment... the apartment actually needs some restructuring, like infrastructure stuff... we have to build another room, and in order to pursue our careers, we have to have another person in our house to help us with the second child... And next year, the school for the first child, the payment goes higher.
anchors.competitor: An apartment renovation, incoming childcare help, and rising school fees
anchors.note: A stack of dated, non-negotiable claims on the same budget, all landing in the same twelve months. Distinct from a general affordability objection because each item resolves on a known schedule, which is what makes the rep's question 'what's going to change between now and sometime in the future?' the right one — and what makes settling for a call in one month the wrong answer, since the prospect's own timeline points past October.

anchors.raw: even job right now, we are changing places and restructuring our private practice. So we may be dealing with a couple of months that money will be a little shorter than it usually is because of that restructuring.
anchors.note: The reason the down-payment question failed. Asked what he could put down today, the prospect could not answer honestly because his income for the next few months is genuinely unknown — 'I may be answering something that is not close to reality if I'm going to just give you a value.' No amount of financial-picture questioning resolves an unknown denominator; what was needed was a hold or deposit mechanism, and none exists.

anchors.raw: after knowing Trevor's YouTube channel, man, I was just very excited to try the tool... I actually was attracted to Trevor's channel, not only by the kettlebells, but by the fasting protocol.
anchors.note: The second instance in this batch, after Marian Samson, of free content building demand rather than substituting for the paid offer. This prospect bought a 16 kg kettlebell because of the channel, adopted the fasting protocol from it, uses Trevor's physique as his goal image, and still concluded he needed paid structure — 'nowadays I can solidly make a workout structure for calisthenic training, but my great doubts nowadays are how to combine those two.' The distinguishing factor across the batch is competence: viewers who can self-programme in the target modality treat the content as a substitute, viewers who cannot treat it as an advertisement.

anchors.raw: she actually likes to train. She likes to run, and she trains CrossFit, and she tries to balance all of that with a career. She is also a doctor and being a mom. So, we try to maintain our level of activity, at least train three to four times a week.
anchors.note: Logged as a supportive anchor precisely because it was never used. The decision was framed as joint ('I have to involve the wife'), and the joint decision-maker is a training doctor who gets frustrated when she cannot train twice a week. She is the single strongest advocate available on this call, her profile was captured in discovery thirty-five minutes before the objection landed, and she was neither discussed after the objection nor invited to the follow-up.

unmet_demand.want: A price that works outside the United States — $6,000 converts to roughly R$25,000-28,000 and $4,000 to about R$20,000 for a Brazilian physician who considers the underlying value fair.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The offer is priced flat in USD with no regional pricing, no purchasing-power adjustment and no framing that addresses conversion when a prospect raises it. This is the third foreign-currency loss in four sales calls in this batch, across New Zealand, Denmark and Brazil, which makes it structural rather than incidental. Whether Primal wants regional pricing is a business decision, but at present the answer to 'that is R$28,000 to me' is silence.

unmet_demand.want: A way to hold or pause the engagement around a scheduled life event — a second child due in the last week of October, with an expected period of severe sleep deprivation either side of it.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: There is no pause, hold or deferred-start mechanism in the offer, and no deposit that reserves a price. The rep improvised the closest available answer, restructuring to a three-month tier to fit the June-to-August window, which was genuinely good thinking — but it still required full payment now against a budget that will not clarify until after the birth. A refundable deposit that locks today's price for a start date in November would have fitted this prospect exactly and does not exist.

unmet_demand.want: Programming that preserves and progresses weighted calisthenics alongside kettlebells — his stated primary condition, raised twice: 'that would be my primary will is to combine those things. To not lose the gains in strength in calisthenics.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Recorded as answered-but-unverified rather than as a failure. The rep's response was good and the objection resolved, but the answer was a promise ('they complement each other naturally', 'this is tailored to your needs, whatever you will discuss with Trevor, he will build a program around that') rather than a specification, and the detail was deferred entirely to the onboarding call. Whether Trevor actually programmes weighted calisthenics progression alongside kettlebell work, or simply absorbs bodyweight movements into kettlebell complexes, is not established anywhere on this call and should be confirmed with a human before the follow-up.

unmet_demand.want: Clarity on what the guarantee actually covers, and why it disappears on the tier being recommended.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The guarantee surfaced here for the first time in the corpus — at least 20 lb, about 10 kg, added to kettlebell working weight from baseline over six months — and was used as an argument for the six-month tier, immediately before the rep recommended the three-month tier which explicitly does not carry it: 'with three months, we cannot guarantee that, because it's too short. I think it's too short for every fitness goal.' The prospect was therefore steered toward the option the rep had just characterised as too short to work. The guarantee's real terms are undocumented and it is not stated on other calls in this batch, including calls selling the same six-month tier.
